old: though case-formation still follows one underlying method, with a more restricted range of alternate forms than classical usage typically shows (two or three variant forms for a single word being common).
new: in word-formation there is a certain order and discipline; in the later language the forms are fewer in number and their formation is harder: where the case-forms had two or three forms there is now only one.
basis: Kannada p.331: roopanishpattiyalli ondu krama; eechina bhasheyalli roopagala sankhye kadime, vibhakti roopagalalli eradu mooru roopa iddalli eega ondu

old: Verb (tiṅanta) forms differ slightly too; the Veda makes wide use of potential/subjunctive-like mood-marking, present in classical Sanskrit only in more limited, indicative-restricted form.
new: Some tiṅanta (finite verb) forms have disappeared altogether. The Veda has one verb-form expressing possibility (the subjunctive), which no longer exists at all; of the eight verb-forms that show only the sense of the action, without gender or number, only one is now in use.
basis: Kannada p.331: tinantaroopagalalliyoo kelavu roopagale illavagive; sambhavanarthaka kriyaroopa eega illave illa; bhavarthada eight forms, one in use

old: The Veda's sandhi (euphonic combination) rules show many differences from classical practice — a few key points are examined below.
new: The Veda also has many varieties of sandhi. Only a few main points are examined here; further grammatical peculiarities will be discussed in detail when they occur in the mantras.
basis: Kannada p.331: sandhigalalliyoo aneka bhedagalu ive; kelavu mukhyamshagalannu mattra; heccige vyakarana visheshanagalu mantragalalli bandaga

old: **Sandhi frequently doesn't occur where classical grammar would expect it**, though it is generally applied throughout the Veda. Classical rule holds that visarga does not occur before consonant-initial words at a word-boundary — but the Veda shows many exceptions, generally where meter demands preserving a required syllable-count; sandhi is even applied mid-word in some cases where meter requires it:
new: **Sandhi often does not occur even where it could** — this is usual in the Veda. Pāṇini's rule is that a short *a* following a word-final *e* or *o* is not pronounced; in writing the avagraha sign is put in its place. Such usage is rare in the Veda; ordinarily the short vowel is pronounced separately. Where the metre needs an extra syllable the *a* is pronounced; where it needs one fewer, the *a* is not pronounced and sandhi occurs:
basis: Kannada p.331: sandhiyagabahudada sandarbhagalalliyoo sandhiyagade iruvudu--vedadalli sadharana; padanta e, o karagala munde baruva hrasva akarakke uccharavillavembudu Paninya niyama; avagraha chihne

old: no sandhi occurs where a word ending in *ī, ū,* or single-mora *ṛ* precedes a following vowel — but the Veda shows many exceptions, especially where the word "iva" follows:
new: there is no sandhi when a vowel follows dual forms ending in *ī, ū* or *e*; but the Veda has many exceptions to this, and where the word *iva* follows, sandhi is certain:
basis: Kannada p.331: ee, oo, ekaranta dvivachana roopagala munde svara bandare sandhiyilla; vedadalli anekā apavadagalu; iva shabda bandalli sandhi siddha

old: In certain consonant contexts, classical rule requires a following "na" sound — but the Veda shows variant forms with na-sound or sha-sound, particularly around the particles "ena" and "ina."
new: Within a single word, an *n* following *ṛ, r* or *ṣ* customarily becomes *ṇ*. In the Veda, however, the *n* becomes *ṇ* even when these sounds stand in different words of one sentence; this applies mostly to the pronoun forms "naḥ" and "ena".
basis: Kannada p.332: ondE padadalli ru, r athava sh ivugalige paravada nakaravu nakaravaguvudu rudhi; vedadalli ... bereberE padagalalliddaroo nakarakke nakaradesha; naha mattu ena

old: Vowel-lengthening for prosodic (metrical) purposes affects words like *atha, adha, pibha, śrutata, vidya, yuṣma, veda, kṛdhi, śṛṇuhi* especially often.
new: A word-final *a* — sometimes *i* and *u* too — is lengthened for the sake of the metre. The words *atha, adha, piba, śṛṇuta, vidma, yuṣva, veda, kṛdhi, śṛṇuhi* are most often subject to this change.
basis: Kannada p.332: atha, adha, piba, shrunuta, vidma, yushva, veda, krdhi, shrunuhi
Kannada p.332 petvena (7-18-17); senena is not in the Kannada

old: both "bhiḥ" and "aiḥ" forms occur — but the "aiḥ" form appears increasingly rarely, surviving mainly among pronominal words:
new: both "ebhiḥ" and "aiḥ" occur; gradually the "ebhiḥ" form became rarer and survives only among pronouns:
basis: Kannada p.333: ebhih mattu aih eradoo; baruburuttta ebhih prayoga kadime agi sarvanamapadagalalli mattra

old: For the **Locative singular**, some words retain the "i"-stem, while a few show a shift to "a"-stem or "ā"-stem-style endings:
new: In the **Locative singular** the *i* becomes *ā* in some places; the locative singular of the word *agni* is in some places *agnā* or *agnāyi*:
basis: Kannada p.333: saptamaikavachanadalli kelavukade ikaravu akaravaguttade; agni shabdada saptamaikavachana agna athava agnayi

new: the final vowel of the stem takes no guṇa, only the case-suffix being added
basis: Kannada p.334: padantasvarakke gunavillade vibhakti pratyaya matra serisibidhuvudu

new: *bhūmīḥ*
basis: Kannada p.334 ಭೂಮಿಾಃ (lengthened i, as the sentence says: dirghavaguvuduntu); bhumyah is not the Kannada form

old: For the second-person plural imperative suffix "mas," the Veda regularly uses "masi" in its place instead — sometimes rendered simply "mas."
new: The first-person plural ending is "mas"; in the Veda "masi" is generally used in its place, and gradually this became rarer until only "mas" is left now.
basis: Kannada p.334: uttamapurusha bahuvachanapratyayavu mas; vedadalli sadharanavagi idara badalu masi; barubarutta kadimeyagi mas ondE eega ulidide

new: ; in later Sanskrit verbs ending in "masi" are not current.
basis: Kannada p.334: eechina samskrutabhasheyalli masi antyavada kriyapadagalu rudhiyallilla

old: For first-person singular Atmanepada verbs, "e" traditionally replaces "i" — but "śṛṇute" appears where "śṛṣṇe" would traditionally be expected instead (7-8-4; 7-26-4).
new: In the third-person singular of the Ātmanepada, "e" sometimes appears in place of the usual ending "te": the form "śṛṇve" appears instead of "śṛṇute" (7-8-4; 7-26-4).
basis: Kannada p.334: atmanepada prathamapurusha ekavachanadalli rudhiyada te pratyayakke badalagi e baruvuduntu; shrunute ge badalagi shrunve

old: The Injunctive mood, middle-voice second-person singular, shows many variant forms — often ending in "dhi" (also seen as "hi," e.g., "śaśādhi," "kṛdhi," "śrudhi" — per Panini, either "dhi" ending is correct). Forms like "śṛṇudhi" and "gṛbhi" also occur.
new: In the imperative, second-person singular, many varieties of forms are found; mostly "dhi" stands at the end: "śaśādhi," "kṛdhi," "śrudhi" and so on (according to Pāṇini, "dhi" should not be added to the last two). Forms like "śṛṇudhi" and "gahi" also occur.
basis: Kannada p.334: ajnartha madhyamapurusha ekavachana; hechchagi dhi; shashadhi, krdhi, shrudhi (Paniniyaprakara iverada kkoo dhi barakoodadu); shrunudhi, gahi

old: In the middle-voice second-person plural, "dhve" and "dhvam" replace classical "dhvam" and "dhvam" variants. Imperative first-person singular forms take an extra "si" suffix — examples: kṣeṣi (7-18-2), bhakṣi (7-41-2), riṣṭi and veśi (7-16-5).
new: In the second-person plural the forms "dhana" and "tana" are also used in place of "tha" and "ta". In the imperative second-person singular the ending "si" is also added — examples: kṣeṣi (7-18-2), bhakṣi (7-41-2), yakṣi and veṣi (7-16-5).
basis: Kannada p.335: madhyamapurusha bahuvachanadalli tha mattu ta ivugalige badalagi dhana mattu tana; ajnartha madhyamapurusha ekavachanakke si; kshesi, bhakshi, yakshi mattu veshi (7-16-5)

old: Present participles occur in many varied forms; the suffix "tam" is generally used, though the Veda uses "avitane" (7-33-1) and "aśnevatane" (7-33-8) in the same sense. Among these:
new: Verbal indeclinables (kṛdanta) are used in many varied forms. The suffix "tum" is still generally in use; in the Veda, in the same sense, forms such as "avitave" (7-33-1) and "anvetave" (7-33-8) are used. Besides these:
basis: Kannada p.335: krdanta avyayagalu; tum pratyaya; avitave (7-33-1), anvetave (7-33-8)

new: - words ending in "tavai": haṃtavai, etavai;
basis: Kannada p.335: tavai antyavada padagalu--hantavai, etavai

new: - words ending in "ase": cakṣase, jīvase;

old: - ending in "taye": pīśhitaye, ūtaye
new: - words ending in "taye": pītaye, ūtaye;
basis: Kannada p.335: taye antyavada--pitaye, utaye

old: - ending in "dhyai": iṣadhyai, sṛṇudhyai, śucidhyai
new: - words ending in "dhyai": iṣadhyai, pṛṇadhyai, śucadhyai;
basis: Kannada p.335: dhai antyavada--ishadhyai, prnadhyai, shuchadhyai

old: - ending in "mane": vitomāḥ, kartomāḥ, and similar forms — all used in the sense of an infinitive.
new: - words ending in "to": etoḥ, kartoḥ, and similar forms — all used in the sense of the bare action (infinitive).
basis: Kannada p.335: to antyavada padagalu--etoh, kartoh modalada roopagalu bhavarthadalli

old: hantvāya, kṛtvī, pītvī, bhūtvī
new: hatvāya, kṛtvī, prītvī, bhūtvī
basis: Kannada p.335: hatvaya, krtvi, pritvi bhutvi

old: **Potential-mood forms** are relatively few; the negating particle "mā" often used alone, combined with root-forms and mood-neutral forms of the base, without the potential-suffix strictly attached — this "mā"-based construction is common in the Veda in the potential sense. The Veda gives such forms the technical name "Let" (imperative/prohibitive). Examples: bhavāti (7-8-6), patāti (7-25-1), tāriṣat, joṣiṣet, mādayaithe — all illustrating this prohibitive/optative-adjacent construction.
new: **The subjunctive verb-form** may be said not to exist at all now. Only when the prohibitive particle "mā" is used are the past and aorist forms used without the initial *a*; this may be said to correspond to the Veda's subjunctive form. Grammarians have given this Vedic form the name "Let". Examples: bhavāti (7-8-6), patāti (7-25-1), tāriṣat, joṣiṣat, mādayyaite, gṛhyāṃtai.
basis: Kannada p.335: sambhavanarthakavada roopavu eega illave illa; maa upayogisidaga mattra bhuta mattu anadyatanabhutakalada roopagalannu adiyalliruva akaravillade; Let; bhavati (7-8-6) patati (7-25-1) tarishat, joshishat, madayyaite, grhyantai

old: ādadhīmahi
new: ādadīmahi
basis: Kannada p.335 adadimahi (indra tvotasa a vayam vajram ghana dadimahi)

old: Comparative-mythology scholars broadly agree the Vedas are extremely ancient.
new: As soon as the Vedas became known, the scholars of the Western countries believed them to be very ancient.
basis: Kannada p.337: vedagala parichayavadodaneye pashchimatyadeshagala panditarugalu vedagalu bahupuratanavendu nambidaru

old: working backward from the known beginning of Buddhism as an anchor point.
new: taking as his basis known events such as Alexander's famous expedition and the beginning of Buddhism.
basis: Kannada p.337: prasiddhavada Alexanderana dandayatre, bauddhamatada prarambha modalada kalagalannu moolavagittukondu

old: Buddhism developed specifically as a reaction against Vedic custom and worldview, its own texts spreading extensively in opposition to Vedic ideology...
new: Buddhism arose as a protest against the Brahmanical or Vedic religion, that is, the religion that follows the practices and conduct stated in the Vedas. By the time Buddhism arose, the Vedas and all the books connected with them must have been in full circulation...
basis: Kannada p.337-338: bauddhamatavu taleyettiduve brahmana athava vaidika matakke pratibhatanaroopavagi...vedagalu mattu adakke sambandhapatta grantha ellavoo sampurnavagi pracharadalliddirabeku

old: since assigning a fixed number of years to each successive textual layer (Samhita, Brahmana, Sutra) has no genuinely scientific basis; civilizational development doesn't proceed in neat, countable increments.
new: since to count two hundred years each for the Samhita, Brahmana and Sutra is unnatural, and two hundred years are not nearly enough for the creation of so much literature.
basis: Kannada p.338: samhita, brahmana, sutragalu ondondakkoo innooru innooru varshagantae ganane madiruvadu asvabhavika; ishtondu sahityasrushtige innooru varsha enenu saladu

old: A merely impressionistic acceptance, without genuine critical examination, isn't appropriate here — though Max Müller's rough 1200 BCE estimate is not accepted point-by-point by everyone, other scholars have arrived at broadly similar figures independently.
new: Even while criticising in a scientific manner, a note of sentiment is seen. Max Müller's statement that the Veda belongs to 1200 BC is no conclusion based on figures; yet it is surprising that scholars gradually come to agree that the date of the Vedas is 1200 BC as he decided, and to take it as the basis of all their discussions.
basis: Kannada p.338: Max Mullerravaru kri. poo. 1200 vedada kalavendu hellirvudu ankiamshagalannusarisiruva nirnayavenoo alla; adaroo baruburutta panditarugaloo...oppuvudoo...ashcharyakara

old: gradual assimilation and cultural spread over generations seems entirely plausible, requiring its own additional span of time to account for — this is **G. Buhler's** view.
new: a country as large as this is impossible; and to conquer people who were uncivilized and quarrelling among themselves, to make them cultured and to spread their literature among them is very hard to achieve. Therefore at least twice that time is needed. This is the view of **G. Buhler**.
basis: Kannada p.340-341: deshavannu gelluvudu asadhya...anagarikaroo parasparakalahamadiddavaroo...durshadhyavadudu...ikke eradarshtadaroo kaala beke beku. idu G. Buhler matha

old: But American linguistic-social change and Indian conditions differ considerably — Vedic-era Aryans maintained a remarkably conservative language and ritual system across generations, treasuring even single words and half-verses of received mantras with great care.
new: But the political situation of America differs greatly from that of India. In the Vedic and Puranic period the occupation of the plains of the Hindu country by the Aryans was a very difficult and slow task; they had to fight for and win every step. Besides, it is known from the Veda that the composition of the Ṛgveda took a long time; among the mantras there are new mantras and old mantras, new ṛṣis and old ṛṣis.
basis: Kannada p.341: americada rajakiya paristhitigoo india deshada paristhitigoo bahala vyatyasa...prati hejjeyannoo avaru kadadi vashapadisikollabekagittu...hosamantra, haleyamantra, hosa rshi, haleya rshi

old: The Rigveda's mantras and those found in other Vedic texts show comparable language, style, and worship-practices with little variation — and the close relationship between Brahmana-texts and their associated shakhas suggests continuous transmission over a considerable span, not a brief one; the Samhita portions cannot simply be assigned to a later era's authorship.
new: The mantras of the Ṛgveda differ in language from the other mantras; the Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads differ from the Saṃhitās in many ways — in language, style, modes of worship and the civilization described. And by the time these Brāhmaṇas and the rest were composed, the four Saṃhitās were in use; moreover, the Saṃhitā portions were not understood at all by many people of that time.
basis: Kannada p.341: rgvedada mantragalige itara mantragaligoo bhasheyalli vyatyasavide...brahmana aranyaka upanishattu ivugaligoo samhitegaligoo aneka vyatyasagalu...nalku samhitegaloo balakeyallittendoo...arthave aguttirallilla

old: The Veda was never composed as a single unified "textbook" — no fixed date can be assigned to it as a whole. But systematic comparison across sources leads most historians to conclude that the Vedic corpus, and its various portions, must span several centuries — the Brahmana literature alone likely took many centuries to fully develop. Some suktas explicitly reference earlier suktas, sometimes naming their composers or patrons directly, confirming relative chronology within the text — the same method used to establish relative dating among Upanishadic teachers' lineages.
new: The Vedas have not come to us in book form. Had writing been in use, the growth of the Vedas would not have needed so much time; but since everything had to be kept in memory and learned by mouth from one person to another, many centuries were needed for the whole Saṃhitā portion to come together. The Brāhmaṇas too must have taken many centuries to take full shape. Considering the many śākhās and sub-śākhās and the countless priests, it is established that all this was not possible in less than several centuries. In the same way, in the Upaniṣads too, differences of time, many generations of teachers and a tradition of centuries are understood.
basis: Kannada p.341: I vedagalu pustakaroopavagi namage bandilla...jnapakadalitukondu bayindale...anekashatamanagalu beku...brahmanagaloo...shakhegalu upashakhegalu lekkavilladashtu jana purohitaru...upanishattugalalliyoo
Kannada p.342: kri. poo. 502 (numerals from the Kannada)

old: Oldenberg and others hold that the Upanishads and early Buddhism are closely connected within a few centuries of each other, even though Buddhism explicitly rejected Vedic textual authority.
new: Oldenberg showed that there must have been a gap of many centuries between the Upanishads and the beginning of Buddhism.
basis: Kannada p.342: Oldenbergravaru upanishattugaligoo bauddhamatada adigoo madhye aneka shatamanagala antaravaddirabekendoo toriddare

old: **G. Buhler** argues this is the correct starting point, and that the Veda's true age must extend considerably further back still.
new: Beginning in this way, **G. Buhler** set out to prove that the Vedas are much earlier than the time now known; unfortunately he died before he could establish his theory.
basis: Kannada p.342: G. Buhlerravaru ee reeti prarambhisi, vedagalu eega tilidiruva kalakkinta bahala hindinavendu sadhisuttenendu horattaru. durdrushtavashat avaru tamma siddhanta sthapisuvadakke modale daivadhinaraadaru

new: **Boghazkoi** in Asia Minor
basis: Kannada p.342: Asia Minor pradeshadalli Boghaskoi emballi; Hattusa is not in the Kannada

old: This discovery has been a matter of major scholarly significance, and its authenticity is universally accepted.
new: Why these names occur in this inscription became a great problem for scholars; each argued in his own way.
basis: Kannada p.342: ee hesarugalu ee shasanadalli baralu karanavenu embudu panditarige doddasamasye ayitu; obbobbaru ondondu reeti vadisiddare

old: the Aryans having crossed through the Mesopotamian region and spread further west before some branch eventually reached India; in his view the composition of the mantras began from about the 17th century BC.
new: by the time the Aryans were spreading in Mesopotamia and Syria they were also spreading in India; in his view the composition of the mantras began from about the 15th century BC onwards.

old: **Oldenberg** shares this view, explicitly rejecting the claim that the Vedas themselves date to this earlier (Mitanni-treaty) period.
new: **Oldenberg** expresses the same opinion and says that there is not enough basis for saying that the Vedas are earlier than this.

new: the Scythian king Kānīta

old: It's not strictly necessary to claim these deities belonged *exclusively* to Vedic worship even at that early date — their worship may have spread into other regions before Vedic tradition, as we know it, later arrived in India along a related cultural stream. Considering this, some scholars in the field hold that an ancient, broadly Vedic-adjacent tradition already existed and extended over a considerable period, well established in various places by about the 14th century BC, with continuous worship-practice for a long time already behind it.
new: It is quite impossible to say that these deities are others than the deities of our Veda. People used to migrate from this country to foreign lands now and then; in the same way people living in India with a Vedic culture may have gone to Asia Minor and other regions. This establishes one point: about the 14th century BC the Aryans had settled in the north-western provinces and had long been engaged in the worship of deities. If it is established from the Asia Minor inscriptions that the numerals of the Hindu country were also in use in that country, our above opinion would be strengthened.
basis: Kannada p.342: ee devategalu namma vedada devategalallade bereyavarendu heluvadu sadhyave illa...kri. poo. sumaru hadinalkaneya shatamanadalli aryaru vayavyaprantagalalli nelesiddaru...ankigalu aa deshadalliddavendu...pushti

old: and the elder-brother-scholar in tradition with Madhavacharya, renowned as a foremost authority across all the shastras, and the author of many independent works.
new: who had an elder brother, Madhavacharya, also a court scholar of King Bukka, unrivalled in all the shastras and the author of many learned works.
basis: Kannada p.344: ivarige Madhavacharyaremba jyeshtha sahodararidduru; avaroo Bukkamaharajana asthanapanditaraagiddaru

old: Recognizing his scholarly mastery, the king asked him to compose a Rigveda commentary for the benefit of the world (lokopakara). Sayana responded: "O great king, you yourself are equal to this task." But the king, though himself accomplished across the shastras, understood the sheer difficulty of Vedic exegesis and judged that undertaking it personally would take far too long — so he turned to Sayanacharya and requested that he take up the work instead.
new: Seeing his scholarship, King Bukka ordered Madhavacharya to write a commentary on the Rigveda for the benefit of the world. Madhavacharya then said to King Bukka: "O great king, I have a younger brother named Sayanacharya. He is expert in all the shastras and knows everything about Vedic matters. If he is ordered to compose the commentary, he will compose it." Accordingly King Bukka summoned Sayanacharya and ordered him to compose a commentary on the Vedas.
basis: Kannada p.344: Bukkamaharajanu lokopakararthavagi Rigvedakke bhashyavannu bareyuvante ajnemadalu, aga avaru (Madhavacharya) Bukkamaharajananna kuritu...nanage Sayanacharyanemba tammaniruvanu...Bukkarajanu Sayanacharyarannu karesi vedabhashyarachanemaduvante appanemadidanu

old: Whichever supreme deity is both the material and efficient cause of the Veda's own form, and whichever supreme soul created, from within the Veda itself, all sentient and insentient beings together with the entire universe — Sayanacharya bows to his own guru Vidyatirtha, regarding him as identical with that very deity, in bodily presence as much as in essence.
new: The Supreme Lord whose breath itself takes the form of the Vedas, and who created the whole universe from the Vedas themselves — that Maheshvara, the master of all the vidyas, or our guru named Vidyatirtha, who is the very form of the Lord, I bow to.
basis: Kannada p.347: yava parameshvarana nishvasagale vedaroopavagiveyo mattu yava paramatmanu vedagalindale samastajagattannu srushtisidano antaha...Maheshvarananna athava sakshadishvarasvaroopanada Vidyatirtharemba namma guruvannu namaskarisuttene

old: For a seeker of knowledge, Indian tradition holds the guru to be worthy of worship equal to the divine itself — "*guru reva maheśvaraḥ*" ("the guru alone is Maheshvara"), as scripture states — and a disciple should regard his guru as identical with Parameshvara (the Supreme Lord) on this basis. This is precisely why Sayanacharya, regarding his own guru Vidyatirtha as one with Ishvara, bows to him here.
new: Vidyatirtha was the guru of Bharatitirtha, and Bharatitirtha was the guru of Madhavacharya; so Vidyatirtha was Madhava's paramaguru. According to the shastra saying "*guru reva maheśvaraḥ*" ("the guru alone is Maheshvara"), the disciple should regard the guru as Parameshvara himself. For these reasons, when Madhavacharya bows to Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara, he bows to both his guru and Maheshvara.
basis: Kannada p.347: Vidyatirtharembuvaru Bharatatirthararembuvarige gurugalu; Bharatatirtharu Madhavacharyarige gurugalu; adudarinda Vidyatirtharu Madhavarige paramagurugalu; gururEva maheshvarah...Madhavacharyaru Vidyatirthamaheshvararannu namaskarisuvaga

old: The Vedas hold the Supreme to be non-dual — "*tat sat, tad vā dvaita*" (that which is Being, whether described as non-dual or dual) — as the Upanishads generally establish. Since the Vedas belong to Parameshvara alone, and since Parameshvara alone created the world and became all beings, and since this same Bhagavan is the ultimate source of all knowledge and every discipline — it follows that, in composing a Veda-commentary, the relationship between every seeker of knowledge and their guru (celebrated as the foremost authority) carries this same weight. With this understanding, Sayana performs his mangalacharana at the very opening of the text.
new: The Vedas are said to be the breath of Parameshvara: an Upanishad passage says that this Rigveda, Yajurveda and Samaveda are the breath of that great Being. Hence the Vedas have come forth from the mouth of the Supreme Self in the form of breath. Moreover, Parameshvara created the world with the help of the Vedas, and this Lord is the cause of all vidyas; from him all vidyas and shastras have arisen. Therefore, at the time of composing the Veda-commentary, Madhavacharya bows to Maheshvara (the guru) renowned by the name Vidyatirtha, who is the very form of all the Vedas and the lord of all vidyas, and so begins the work after making the auspicious invocation of bowing to Ishvara and the guru.
